text.content:
Create an NPC the same way as a Character — from the Actors sidebar's Create Actor button, with Type set to NPC / Adversary. NPCs use the exact same Attributes, Skills, Resources, Wounds, and Combat Dice as player characters; they just skip the player-facing fields (Concept, Career, Non-Combat Skills) in favor of a Role tag (Minion/Standard/Elite/Nemesis) and a GM Notes field for tactics reminders.

Leave NPC tokens unlinked (Foundry's default) so multiple copies of the same monster track their own Wounds independently. Character tokens are force-linked instead, since a PC should always be the same Actor everywhere.

Portrait Art vs. Token Art

Every Actor has two separate images: the sheet Portrait (click the art in the header) and the canvas Token Image. Foundry copies your Portrait into the Token Image automatically the first time you set one — after that, the two are independent, so changing one later never touches the other. Use the small pawn icon on the Portrait's corner to set the Token Image directly. Since NPC tokens are unlinked, updating an NPC's Token Image only affects tokens you place after the change; drag a fresh one from the sheet, or right-click a placed token → Configure Token to update it individually.

Combat runs entirely through Foundry's own Combat Tracker — add combatants, click Begin Combat, and advance rounds and turns from there. Every way of rolling Initiative (the tracker's dice icon, its Roll All/Roll NPCs buttons, or a sheet's own button) opens the same dice-commit prompt and works identically, so it doesn't matter which one anyone uses.

Deleting the Combat (ending Foundry's tracker) resets each combatant's per-Combat state — Action/Reaction Dice, Round-based Card cooldowns, and so on. It does not by itself end the fictional Encounter: V6 treats Combat starting and stopping inside the same ongoing Encounter as normal (an ambush that pauses and resumes, say), so anything scoped to the Encounter — Threads, Authority, per-Encounter Card cooldowns, a Reach Trigger's "usable only this Encounter" duration — stays in effect across that gap. Only clicking a sheet's own New Encounter button clears those; use it once you and the table agree the Encounter itself, not just one bout of Combat, is actually over.

Conditions live in the Conditions compendium and double as Token HUD status icons — right-click a token, open its status-effects palette, and toggle a Condition directly. This adds or removes a real owned Condition item on the Actor, with whatever mechanical effect the rules define (Chilled's Movement penalty, for instance), exactly the same as dragging the Condition onto the sheet by hand. Each Condition Item carries a Classification (Ordinary/Specialty/Wound/Influence Consequence/Cover/Other) purely as a sheet label — nothing in the module branches on it, it just says which V6 subsystem the Condition belongs to.

Stacking, Reapplication, and Participation

Differently named Conditions stack. The same named ordinary Condition does not stack with itself — reapplying it refreshes its duration rather than increasing its magnitude. Ordinary Condition removal never removes a Wound Condition or a Specialty Condition unless it explicitly says it can. A Condition restricts only the capabilities its own entry names; apply that restriction while letting the character use their remaining Actions, Reactions, and Movement normally — Conditions are not a general-purpose way to skip a character's Turn.

Authoring New Content

If you have Foundry's "Create Items" permission, a wand-icon scene-control button opens the Create Content wizard for building new Action/Reaction Cards, Equipment, and Conditions straight into the compendium — no hand-editing the data model required. For adding many at once, use its Bulk Import option: download a CSV template, fill it out, and upload it to create or update several items in one pass.

Compendiums

Species, Heritages, and Distinctions are hand-authored. The Combat Styles Reference and Full Manifestation Guide journals document their respective mechanics in full. See the system's README if you need to know where a given compendium's content actually comes from.

Every NPC carries a Role tag — Minion, Standard, Elite, or Nemesis. The Monster Creator's Auto-Generate Stat Block button uses a tunable budget table (four Roles, seven axes each) to fill one out for you in seconds, then hands every result back for you to hand-edit like anything else on the sheet.

RoleAttributesSkillsResilienceTemp WoundsCards (A/R)Equipment
Minion2 pts, max 22 pts, max 21 + 1×Tier01 / 01
Standard7 pts, max 35 pts, max 33 + 2×Tier12 / 12
Elite10 pts, max 48 pts, max 45 + 3×Tier23 / 23
Nemesis13 pts, max 512 pts, max 57 + 4×Tier34 / 34

Auto-Generate rolls, in order: a weighted Attribute/Skill point-buy (leaning toward whichever domain you pick as Emphasis, respecting the same five Distinction gates a player would), Resilience/Temp Wounds/Equipment Limit straight from the table above, a set of qualifying Combat Cards weighted toward the Skills that rolled highest, and a random Equipment draw. Each step has its own Reroll button if you just want to redo one part.

Treat this table as a starting point, not a law — every number lives in module/data/monster-budgets.mjs and takes effect immediately if you tune it.
